source.title: Does the Model Use the Feature? Separating Steering from Mechanism in LLMs

record.tranche_reason: The study's own interventions and results argue that feature tracking or strong steering alone does not establish that a model uses a feature; the mechanistic conclusion depends on natural-value tests and the intervention details.
record.gate_note: The paper tests SAE latents, dense directions and an agreement feature set as candidate mechanisms, not neuron poles, neuron job counts, attribution graphs, or explanation scores for predicting activations. Its feature-level results are recorded as related findings that do not match a listed version. Cited results from other studies are not recorded.
record.test_reason: The study tests whether SAE latents, dense directions and an SAE feature set are used by the model at natural values (installation, removal, rescue). It never audits neuron poles, counts neuron jobs, scores neuron explanations, or builds neuron attribution graphs. Its results therefore bear on no listed version. The reader's 'tests'/T5 is wrong: the T5 argument is about steering-versus-mechanism for features, not about the neuron claims. Neither original source is cited.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. Association and steering do not show that a model uses a feature. Natural-value installation, removal and rescue give representation-dependent results, and claims must specify representation, site, tokens, update rule and measure.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses paired interchange and downstream rescue on SAE latents, dense directions and a multi-site SAE feature set; it does not perform neuron-pole job audits, explanation scoring, or attribution-graph reconstruction.
record.method_sensitivity: The results vary with representation (SAE latent versus dense direction), model, feature-set update rule (decoder versus encoder-constrained), intervention type (installation, removal, rescue), site and edited tokens. The refusal-control effect also differs between a one-site/token edit and ablation at every layer and position.

fits_no_version.finding: Published Gemma entity SAE latents separate known from unknown entities and strongly steer abstention out of range. At natural values they transfer little of the abstention contrast, and the known-entity latent does not carry the alias accuracy gain.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A feature can track a concept and steer behaviour while carrying little of the natural behavioural contrast.

fits_no_version.finding: Dense known–unknown directions show opposite installation/removal asymmetries in Llama and Gemma. The Pythia agreement feature set shows high sufficiency and use, but installation and rescue depend on the update rule.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Feature sufficiency and use dissociate across representations and depend on the update rule used to write values.

record.code_released: The complete experimental codebase will be released upon publication; no URL stated.
record.problems: The paper does not test the neuron-level claims in the prompt. The Gemma latent interchange intervals include zero, rescue was not run for the two individual Gemma latents, and the agreement-feature positive case is in Pythia-70M-deduped rather than a large modern model. The entity-response judge was checked against human labels, but the audit's behavioral outcomes still depend on the stated response-classification rubric.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-version result was omitted. The refusal-direction positive control and its one-site versus all-layer ablations were left out because they test instruction refusal rather than the listed neuron interpretability claims. Random matched-feature-set control values are noted under r24 but not added as separate rows.

untested.parts: No Qwen3-32B neuron-pole audit or shares of one/two/unknown jobs.
No neuron-job shares across models, dense vs MoE, or scale.
No InceptionV1 or canonical polysemantic neuron analysis.
No comparison of architecture, regularization or tools against interpretable-neuron share.
No neuron-based attribution graphs versus replacement models.
No test of whether activating-example explanations predict neuron firing.
No simulation-based scoring of neuron explanations.

record.verdict_notes: The study is about the validity of causal claims for SAE features and directions. It is adjacent to interpretability claims but not to the neuron-cleanliness versions. No verdicts are given.

versions.untested_parts: Does not audit Qwen3-32B neuron poles or estimate shares with one, two, or unknown jobs.
Does not measure neuron-job shares across model sizes, dense versus mixture-of-experts models, or trillion-parameter models.
Does not study InceptionV1 cat-and-car neurons, pose, or recursive generalization.
Does not compare architectures, regularization, or tools for interpretable-neuron shares.
Does not test attribution graphs built from a large model's own neurons or compare them with a trained replacement model and reconstruction error.
Does not test whether an explanation fitted to a neuron's activating examples predicts where that neuron fires.
Does not score neuron explanations by simulating activations on new text or report the share achieving good scores.
